skills.title: Locate and name India's major physical regions on a map (Himalayas, Northern Plains, Thar Desert, Peninsular Plateau, Coastal Plains, Islands)
Describe the key features of each region (height, rock and soil, rivers)
Explain how a region's land and rivers shape ways of life (farming, homes, food, clothes, travel)
Compare two regions and apply the ideas to one's own area

expectations: India has very different physical regions: the Himalayan mountains in the north, the Northern (Indo-Gangetic) Plains, the Thar Desert in the north-west, the Peninsular (Deccan) Plateau in the south, coastal plains along the east and west coasts, and two island groups (Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep).
The Himalayas are young, very high fold mountains; snow- and glacier-fed rivers such as the Ganga, Yamuna and Brahmaputra begin there and flow all year.
The Northern Plains are flat and made of fertile soil (alluvium) laid down by rivers, so they support farming and a large population.

The Peninsular Plateau is old, hard rock, higher than the plains and edged by the Western and Eastern Ghats; most of its big rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal; the Thar is dry and sandy but people, animals and plants live there.
Land and climate together shape how people live (crops, house design, clothes, food, travel); people adapt to the land and also change it.

items.prompt_en: Name the six major physical regions of India.
items.prompt_hi: India ke chhah bade bhautik kshetra (physical regions) ke naam batao.
items.answer: Himalayan mountains, Northern Plains, Thar Desert, Peninsular Plateau, Coastal Plains, Islands.
acceptable: mountains, plains, desert, plateau, coasts, islands
Himalaya, maidan, registaan, pathaar, tat, dweep
hints: Think of a train journey from Kashmir to Kanyakumari
Start at the top: snowy mountains, then flat land…
Prompt: mountains, plains, ___, plateau, ___, islands
Assert: Himalayas, Northern Plains, Thar, Peninsular Plateau, Coastal Plains, Islands

verified.solverAnswer: Himalayas, Northern Plains, Thar Desert, Peninsular Plateau, Coastal Plains, Islands

items.prompt_en: You take a train from Delhi to Chennai. Using a physical map, describe in words which kinds of land you would pass through.
items.prompt_hi: Tum Delhi se Chennai train se jaa rahe ho. Physical map dekh ke shabdon mein batao ki raaste mein kaun-kaun si zameen aayegi.
items.answer: Flat Northern Plains around Delhi, then hilly central highlands, then the Peninsular (Deccan) Plateau, and finally the low Eastern Coastal Plain near Chennai.
acceptable: plains, hills, plateau, then coast
maidan, pahadiyan, pathaar, phir samudri tat
hints: Look at the colours along the route: green, then yellow-brown…
Green on a physical map means low land; brown means higher land
Prompt: start on the flat ___, cross the ___, end on the eastern ___
Assert: plains → central highlands → Deccan Plateau → Eastern Coastal Plain

verified.solverAnswer: Northern Plains -> central highlands (Vindhya/Satpura area) -> Deccan Plateau -> Eastern Coastal Plain

items.prompt_en: Why is the soil of the Northern Plains so good for farming?
items.prompt_hi: Uttari maidanon (Northern Plains) ki mitti kheti ke liye itni achhi kyun hai?
items.answer: It is alluvial soil: fine, fertile soil carried down from the Himalayas and spread by rivers like the Ganga, Yamuna and Brahmaputra.
acceptable: rivers brought fertile alluvium
nadiyon ne upjaau mitti bichhayi
alluvial soil
hints: Where does this soil come from?
Think about what rivers carry when they flood
Prompt: rivers carry fine ___ from the mountains and spread it on the ___
Assert: rivers deposit fertile alluvium across the flat plains

verified.solverAnswer: Fertile alluvial soil deposited by Himalayan rivers on flat land

items.prompt_en: Why do the Ganga and Yamuna have water all year, while many Deccan rivers become thin in summer?
items.prompt_hi: Ganga aur Yamuna mein saal bhar paani kyun rehta hai, jabki Deccan ki kai nadiyaan garmi mein patli ho jaati hain?
items.answer: Himalayan rivers are fed by melting snow and glaciers as well as rain, so they flow all year; most Deccan rivers depend only on monsoon rain.
acceptable: snow-fed vs rain-fed
barf pighalne se paani milta hai, Deccan ki nadiyaan sirf baarish par
glaciers melt in summer
hints: Where do these rivers start?
What is on top of the Himalayas even in summer?
Prompt: Himalayan rivers get water from melting ___; Deccan rivers mostly from ___
Assert: snow- and glacier-fed rivers are perennial; rain-fed rivers shrink in the dry season

verified.solverAnswer: Himalayan rivers are snow/glacier-fed and perennial; Deccan rivers are rain-fed

items.prompt_en: Predict: what would happen to farms and towns in the Northern Plains if many Himalayan glaciers shrank a lot?
items.prompt_hi: Socho: agar Himalaya ke bahut saare glacier bahut chhote ho jaayein, toh Northern Plains ke kheton aur shehron ka kya hoga?
items.answer: Rivers would carry less water in the dry months, so there would be less water for irrigation and drinking, and crops and towns would suffer.
acceptable: rivers dry up in summer, less water for farms
garmi mein nadiyon mein paani kam, kheti ko nuksaan
water shortage
hints: What feeds these rivers in summer?
If that source becomes small, what happens to river water?
Prompt: less melting ice means less ___ in the rivers, so less ___ for fields
Assert: shrinking glaciers mean less dry-season river water for farms and cities

verified.solverAnswer: Less dry-season river water -> irrigation and drinking-water shortages (after a phase of more meltwater/floods)

items.prompt_en: Many traditional houses in the Thar have thick mud walls and small windows. Why?
items.prompt_hi: Thar ke bahut se purane gharon ki deewarein mitti ki moti aur khidkiyaan chhoti hoti hain. Kyun?
items.answer: Thick mud walls and small windows keep out the strong daytime heat and hot sandy winds, and keep the house warmer during cold desert nights.
acceptable: to keep heat and sand out
garmi aur dhool andar na aaye
cool by day, warm at night
hints: What is the weather like in the desert by day and by night?
Thick walls slow down heat going in and out
Prompt: thick walls keep the ___ out by day and the ___ in at night
Assert: the design is an adaptation to heat, sandstorms and cold nights

verified.solverAnswer: Thick walls/small windows keep out daytime heat and sand, keep warmth in on cold nights

items.prompt_en: Someone says the Thar Desert is empty and nothing can live there. Give three examples that show people, animals and plants do live there, and how they manage with little water.
items.prompt_hi: Koi kehta hai ki Thar registaan khaali hai aur wahan kuch nahi reh sakta. Teen example do jo dikhayein ki wahan log, jaanwar aur paudhe rehte hain, aur kam paani mein kaise guzaara karte hain.
items.answer: People live in villages and towns (like Jaisalmer and Barmer), store rainwater in underground tanks (tankas) and grow hardy crops like bajra; camels can go many days without water; khejri trees have deep roots and give fodder and shade.
acceptable: villages with tankas and bajra, camels, khejri trees
hints: Think of a camel and why it suits the desert
How could a family save the little rain that falls?
Prompt: people store water in ___, camels ___, and trees like ___ have deep roots
Assert: the Thar is home to people, animals and plants adapted to dryness

verified.solverAnswer: Villages like Jaisalmer/Barmer, tankas for rainwater, bajra; camels and goats; khejri/cactus with deep roots

items.prompt_en: Compare life in a village in Ladakh with life in a village in the Ganga plains: one difference each in crops, houses and travel.
items.prompt_hi: Ladakh ke ek gaon aur Ganga ke maidan ke ek gaon ki zindagi compare karo: fasal, ghar aur safar mein ek-ek fark batao.
items.answer: Ladakh: cold, dry, high — barley and apricots, short growing season; flat-roofed stone or mud-brick houses with thick walls; mountain roads and passes closed by snow in winter. Ganga plains: hot summers, fertile flat land — rice, wheat, sugarcane; brick houses, often sloping roofs; easy flat roads and railways.
acceptable: Ladakh barley, cold houses, snowy passes; plains rice-wheat, flat roads
pahad mein jau, maidan mein dhaan-gehun
hints: Start with temperature and height in each place
Which crops need warm, wet, flat land?
Prompt: Ladakh grows ___ and has ___ roads; the plains grow ___ and have ___ roads
Assert: height and cold shape Ladakh; flat fertile land shapes the plains

verified.solverAnswer: Ladakh: barley, thick-walled flat-roofed houses, passes snowbound; plains: rice/wheat, brick houses, easy roads/rail

items.prompt_en: Think about your own town or village. Which physical region is it in? Give two ways the land or rivers there shape what people grow, eat or do for work.
items.prompt_hi: Apne shehar ya gaon ke baare mein socho. Woh kis physical region mein hai? Do tareeke batao jinse wahan ki zameen ya nadiyaan logon ki kheti, khaana ya kaam-dhandha tay karti hain.
items.answer: A correct answer names the right region for the child's place and gives two real links between landform/rivers and life (e.g. coastal town → fishing and coconut; plains → wheat and rice farming; plateau → cotton on black soil; hills → terrace farming, tea).
acceptable: any correct region plus two valid land-life links
hints: Where is your town on the map: near mountains, sea, river or flat land?
What do many people around you grow or sell?
Prompt: my town is in the ___, so people ___ and ___
Assert: name the region, then link one landform feature to one way of life, twice

verified.solverAnswer: Open: correct region + two land-life links

items.prompt_en: Find the mistakes: "The Deccan Plateau is a young mountain range made of soft soil brought by rivers, and its big rivers all flow west."
items.prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: "Deccan Pathaar ek nayi parvat shrinkhla hai jo nadiyon ki laayi naram mitti se bani hai, aur iski saari badi nadiyaan pashchim ki taraf behti hain."
items.answer: The Deccan is an old plateau of hard rock (not a young mountain range of soft river soil); most of its big rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi) flow east into the Bay of Bengal — only a few, like the Narmada and Tapi, flow west.
acceptable: old hard-rock plateau, rivers mostly flow east
purana kathor chattano wala pathaar, nadiyaan poorab ki taraf
hints: Is the plateau young or old? Soft or hard?
Which sea do the Godavari and Kaveri reach?
Prompt: the Deccan is an ___ plateau of ___ rock, and most rivers flow ___
Assert: old, hard rock, rivers mostly eastward (Narmada and Tapi are the westward exceptions)

verified.solverAnswer: Deccan is an old hard-rock plateau, not young soft mountains; most rivers flow east (Narmada/Tapi west)

items.prompt_en: On a physical map, one line of hills runs unbroken close to the west coast; another runs broken into pieces along the east. Name each and say why the eastern one is broken.
items.prompt_hi: Physical map par ek pahadiyon ki line pashchimi tat ke paas bina toote chalti hai; doosri poorab mein tukdon mein bati hai. Dono ke naam batao aur poorvi wali tooti kyun hai?
items.answer: The unbroken western line is the Western Ghats (Sahyadri); the broken eastern line is the Eastern Ghats, cut through by big east-flowing rivers like the Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi and Kaveri.
acceptable: Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats; rivers cut the eastern ones
Pashchimi Ghat, Poorvi Ghat; nadiyon ne kaata
hints: "Ghat" is the name for these hill lines
Which way do the Deccan rivers flow, and what is in their way?
Prompt: the western line is the ___ Ghats; the eastern one is cut by ___
Assert: Western Ghats unbroken; Eastern Ghats broken by east-flowing rivers

verified.solverAnswer: Western Ghats continuous; Eastern Ghats broken by east-flowing rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri)

items.prompt_en: Teach a cousin from another country why India is called a land of geographical diversity. Use at least three regions and say how life differs in each.
items.prompt_hi: Videsh mein rehne wale apne cousin ko samjhao ki India ko bhaugolik vividhta (geographical diversity) wala desh kyun kehte hain. Kam se kam teen regions lo aur batao wahan zindagi kaise alag hai.
items.answer: Key idea: India has mountains, plains, desert, plateau, coasts and islands side by side; each has different height, soil, rivers and climate, which leads to different crops, homes, food and work.

hints: Which three places would you show first?
For each: what is the land like, and what do people do there?
Prompt: in the ___ people ___ because the land is ___
Assert: diversity = many landforms → many ways of living, in one country

verified.solverAnswer: Open: three regions, landform -> different life

items.prompt_en: Why do so many people live in the Northern Plains?
items.prompt_hi: Northern Plains mein itne saare log kyun rehte hain?
items.answer: The land is flat and fertile with rivers that flow all year, so farming is easy and food is plentiful; flat land also makes roads, railways, towns and trade easy.

zameen samtal, upjaau, paani bharpoor
hints: What do people need to settle and grow food?
Think of soil, water and how easy it is to build roads
Prompt: the land is ___, the soil is ___, and rivers give ___

items.prompt_en: A trekker starts at Dehradun (about 650 m high) and climbs to a pass about 4,000 m high. Predict: will it get warmer or colder as she climbs? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Ek trekker Dehradun (lagbhag 650 m) se chal ke lagbhag 4,000 m oonche darre tak chadhti hai. Socho: oopar jaate hue thand badhegi ya garmi? Kyun?
items.answer: Colder: air temperature falls as height increases (roughly 6 °C for every 1,000 m), so at 4,000 m it is much colder even though she is "closer to the sun".

thand badhegi kyunki oonchai par hawa thandi hoti hai
hints: Think of a hill-station trip — did you need a sweater?
Does being a few km closer to the sun matter when the sun is millions of km away?
Prompt: as you go ___, the air gets ___
Assert: higher altitude → colder air

verified.solverAnswer: Colder; temperature falls with altitude (~6.5 C per km)

skills.title: Tell weather (short-term) apart from climate (long-term average)
Name the elements of weather and the instrument that measures each
Explain how weather elements are linked (heating, pressure, wind, humidity, rain)
Read and act on a weather report or IMD forecast and alert

expectations: Weather is the condition of the air at a place for a short time (hours or days); climate is the average weather pattern of a place over a long time (about 30 years or more).
The elements of weather are temperature, air pressure, wind (speed and direction), humidity, precipitation (rain, snow, hail) and clouds.
Each element is measured with an instrument: thermometer (temperature), barometer (air pressure), anemometer (wind speed), wind vane (wind direction), rain gauge (rainfall), hygrometer (humidity).

The elements are linked: the sun heats land and air unevenly; warm air rises and makes low pressure; air moves from high to low pressure as wind; warm air can hold more water vapour, and when moist air rises and cools, clouds and rain form.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) gathers data from weather stations, satellites and radar to make forecasts and colour-coded alerts that help farmers, fishers, pilots and families plan and stay safe.

misconceptions.belief: Weather and climate mean the same thing.
signs: Says "today's climate is rainy"
Thinks one cold day changes a city's climate
Uses the two words interchangeably

diagnostic.prompt_en: Mumbai had an unusually cool, dry day last January. What can we say?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Pichhli January mein Mumbai mein ek din achaanak thanda aur sookha tha. Isse kya pata chalta hai?

options.text: That was the weather that day; Mumbai's climate is still warm and humid
Mumbai's climate has become cold
Climate changes every day, so both are the same

verified.solverAnswer: That was the weather that day; Mumbai's climate is still warm and humid
verified.note: Exactly one correct option; distractors plausible and one maps to this misconception. Correct option is listed first (runtime shuffles per lesson).

misconceptions.belief: Wind is made by trees waving their branches (or by clouds pushing air).
signs: Says trees "make" the wind
Thinks wind stops where there are no trees
Cannot link wind to heating or pressure

diagnostic.prompt_en: What actually causes wind?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Hawa (wind) asal mein chalti kyun hai?

options.text: Air moving from high pressure to low pressure because places heat up unevenly
Trees waving their branches
Clouds pushing the air along

verified.solverAnswer: Air moving from high pressure to low pressure because places heat up unevenly
verified.note: Exactly one correct option; distractors plausible and one maps to this misconception. Correct option is listed first (runtime shuffles per lesson).

remediation.representation: Balloon-and-tyre picture: squeezed air rushing out from where it is packed (high pressure) to where there is room (low pressure); a sea-breeze diagram with arrows
remediation.moveShape: Ask what happens to wind on a treeless beach or desert; then build the heating → rising air → low pressure → wind chain with the child

diagnostic.prompt_en: Chennai in May feels very sticky and sweaty, but it has not rained. Which element is high?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Mai mein Chennai bahut chipchipa aur paseene wala lagta hai, par baarish nahi hui. Kaunsa element zyada hai?

options.text: Humidity — a lot of invisible water vapour in the air
Rainfall
Air pressure only

verified.solverAnswer: Humidity — a lot of invisible water vapour in the air
verified.note: Exactly one correct option; distractors plausible and one maps to this misconception. Correct option is listed first (runtime shuffles per lesson).

remediation.representation: Cold-glass demo: drops appear on a cold glass from invisible vapour in the air, without any rain
remediation.moveShape: Run the cold-glass observation; separate "water in the air" (humidity) from "water falling" (rain)

items.prompt_en: In one line each, what is weather and what is climate?
items.prompt_hi: Ek-ek line mein batao: weather (mausam) kya hai aur climate (jalvaayu) kya hai?
items.answer: Weather is the condition of the air at a place for a short time; climate is the average weather of a place over a long time (about 30 years or more).
acceptable: weather = short time, climate = long-term average
mausam aaj ka, jalvaayu saalon ka average
hints: Which one changes from morning to evening?
Which one describes a place over many years?
Prompt: weather is ___-term; climate is the ___ over many years
Assert: weather = now; climate = long-term average

verified.solverAnswer: Weather = short-term state of atmosphere; climate = long-term (~30 yr) average

items.prompt_en: Sort these into weather or climate: (a) It is raining in Pune right now. (b) Rajasthan is dry most of the year. (c) Puri will be windy tomorrow. (d) Shillong has cool summers.
items.prompt_hi: Inko weather ya climate mein baanto: (a) Pune mein abhi baarish ho rahi hai. (b) Rajasthan saal ke zyaadatar samay sookha rehta hai. (c) Kal Puri mein tez hawa chalegi. (d) Shillong ki garmiyaan thandi hoti hain.
items.answer: Weather: (a) and (c). Climate: (b) and (d).
acceptable: a, c weather; b, d climate
hints: Look for time words: "right now", "tomorrow", "most of the year"
Short time → weather; long-term pattern → climate
Prompt: (a) and (c) talk about ___; (b) and (d) talk about ___
Assert: a, c are weather; b, d are climate

verified.solverAnswer: a, c weather; b, d climate

items.prompt_en: Match each instrument to what it measures: thermometer, barometer, anemometer, wind vane, rain gauge, hygrometer.
items.prompt_hi: Har instrument ko uske naap se milao: thermometer, barometer, anemometer, wind vane, rain gauge, hygrometer.
items.answer: Thermometer – temperature; barometer – air pressure; anemometer – wind speed; wind vane – wind direction; rain gauge – rainfall; hygrometer – humidity.
acceptable: thermo-temp, baro-pressure, anemo-wind speed, vane-direction, gauge-rain, hygro-humidity
hints: "Thermo" is about heat; "baro" is about pressure
Spinning cups count how fast the wind blows
Prompt: the ___ shows which way the wind comes from; the ___ catches rain
Assert: list all six pairs

verified.solverAnswer: thermometer-temperature, barometer-pressure, anemometer-wind speed, wind vane-direction, rain gauge-rainfall, hygrometer-humidity

items.prompt_en: Find the mistakes: "Ravi measured wind speed with a wind vane and rainfall with a thermometer."
items.prompt_hi: Galti pakdo: "Ravi ne hawa ki speed wind vane se naapi aur baarish thermometer se."
items.answer: Wind speed is measured with an anemometer (a wind vane shows direction), and rainfall with a rain gauge (a thermometer measures temperature).
acceptable: anemometer for speed, rain gauge for rain
hints: What does a wind vane point to?
What does a thermometer read?
Prompt: speed needs an ___; rain needs a ___
Assert: anemometer → speed; rain gauge → rainfall

verified.solverAnswer: Wind speed needs anemometer; rainfall needs rain gauge

items.prompt_en: On a sunny afternoon at the beach, a cool breeze blows from the sea onto the land. Explain why.
items.prompt_hi: Dhoop wali dopahar ko beach par samundar se zameen ki taraf thandi hawa chalti hai. Kyun?
items.answer: Land heats up faster than water; warm air over the land rises, creating lower pressure there; cooler, higher-pressure air over the sea moves in to replace it — the sea breeze.
acceptable: land heats faster, air rises, sea air moves in
zameen jaldi garam, hawa upar uthi, samundar ki hawa aayi
hints: Which gets hot faster in the sun: sand or sea water?
What does warm air do?
Prompt: warm air over the ___ rises, making ___ pressure; air from the ___ rushes in
Assert: uneven heating → pressure difference → wind from sea to land

verified.solverAnswer: Land heats faster -> low pressure over land -> sea air moves in (sea breeze)

items.prompt_en: Now predict: at night, which way will the breeze blow at the same beach? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Ab socho: raat ko usi beach par hawa kis taraf chalegi? Kyun?
items.answer: From the land to the sea (a land breeze), because land cools faster than water at night, so the air over the sea is warmer and rises, making lower pressure over the sea.
acceptable: land to sea, land cools faster
zameen se samundar ki taraf
hints: Which cools down faster after sunset?
Where will the warmer, rising air be at night?
Prompt: at night the ___ is warmer, so air moves from ___ to ___
Assert: night → land breeze, from land to sea

verified.solverAnswer: Land breeze, land to sea; land cools faster at night

items.prompt_en: There are no trees in the middle of the sea, yet strong winds blow there. What does this tell you about what causes wind?
items.prompt_hi: Beech samundar mein ek bhi ped nahi hota, phir bhi wahan tez hawa chalti hai. Isse hawa ke kaaran ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
items.answer: Trees do not make wind; wind is air moving from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure, caused by uneven heating by the sun.
acceptable: air moves from high to low pressure
hawa high pressure se low pressure ki taraf jaati hai

skills.title: Explain the factors that control climate: latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, mountains (relief) and winds
Explain how the monsoon works: uneven heating, the south-west monsoon and the retreating (north-east) monsoon
Describe India's seasons and climatic regions and read them from a map or rainfall chart
Explain how climate shapes life and how climate change is affecting it

expectations: Climate differs across India because of latitude (the Tropic of Cancer runs across the middle), altitude (higher places are colder), distance from the sea (coasts are milder, interiors have hotter summers and colder winters) and mountains that block or lift winds.

"Monsoon" means a seasonal reversal of winds: in summer the land heats more than the sea, low pressure forms over north-west India, and moist south-west winds from the Indian Ocean bring most of India's rain, roughly June to September.
When moist winds are forced up mountains (Western Ghats, Khasi hills) they cool and drop heavy rain on the windward side; the far side gets much less (rain shadow).
From about October to December the winds reverse; the retreating or north-east monsoon brings rain to the Tamil Nadu coast; India has winter, summer, monsoon and post-monsoon seasons.
Climate shapes crops, homes, clothes, food and festivals; climate change is making heatwaves, very heavy rain and erratic monsoons more frequent, which affects farmers and cities.

expectations: After the Harappan cities declined (from about 1900 BCE), people lived mainly in villages for many centuries; around 600 BCE (the 6th century BCE) cities grew again, especially in the Ganga plains.

A janapada was the land where a jana (a people) settled; some became large and powerful mahajanapadas — Buddhist and Jain texts list sixteen, such as Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti, Vajji and Gandhara.
Some mahajanapadas were kingdoms ruled by a raja; others were gana-sanghas, where many leaders took decisions together in an assembly, like the Vajji sangha with its capital at Vaishali.
Iron tools helped clear land and grow extra food (a surplus); this supported crafts, trade, taxes, armies and fortified capitals such as Rajagriha.
We know this from texts, from archaeology (fort walls, pottery, tools) and from the earliest Indian coins, the punch-marked coins; in BCE dates, a bigger number means earlier.

expectations: Magadha became the strongest mahajanapada thanks to fertile Ganga plains, rivers for transport and defence, iron ore for tools and weapons, forests with elephants for the army, and ambitious rulers; its capital moved from Rajagriha to Pataliputra.

Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya (Kautilya), overthrew the Nanda rulers around 321 BCE and founded the Mauryan empire, the first to cover most of the subcontinent; Bindusara and then Ashoka followed.

The empire was run from Pataliputra through provinces, officials, tax collectors, a large army and spies; the Arthashastra (a text on running a state) and the accounts of Megasthenes, a Greek envoy, are among our sources.

After the bloody Kalinga war (around 261 BCE), Ashoka turned to dhamma: non-violence, respect for elders and teachers, tolerance for all faiths, and kindness to people and animals; he spread it through edicts carved on rocks and pillars, mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script.
Ashoka's lion capital from Sarnath is India's national emblem and the Ashoka Chakra is on the national flag; historians read edicts carefully because they give the ruler's own point of view.

expectations: The Gupta dynasty rose in the Ganga plains around 320 CE under Chandragupta I; Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta and Skandagupta followed; sources include the Prayag (Allahabad) pillar inscription by the court poet Harishena, coins, and the account of the Chinese traveller Faxian.

Metal-workers made the iron pillar now at Mehrauli in Delhi, which has hardly rusted in about 1,600 years.

In art and literature, Kalidasa wrote Sanskrit plays and poems such as Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghaduta; the Ajanta cave paintings date from around this time (under the Vakatakas, allies of the Guptas); early stone temples (like Deogarh) were built; Nalanda began to grow as a centre of learning.

Creativity flourished because of royal patronage, wealth from farming and trade, relative peace in the core regions and centres of learning; historians debate calling it a "golden age", since life for ordinary people was not the same as for courts and elites.

skills.title: Explain what makes a place sacred: natural features (rivers, confluences, mountains, groves) and links to saints, teachers or events
Locate and describe sacred and pilgrimage sites of different traditions across India
Explain how pilgrimage connected people and regions across India
Explain how reverence for nature helps protect it, and the challenges sacred places face today

expectations: A place becomes sacred when people link it with the divine, a saint, a teacher or an important event; very often these are natural features — rivers and their confluences (sangam), mountains, caves, lakes, springs and forests.

Many traditions have sacred places spread across India: for example the Char Dham at four corners (Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, Rameswaram), the Kumbh Mela sites (Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, Nashik), Bodh Gaya and Sarnath for Buddhists, Sammed Shikhar and Shravanabelagola for Jains, the Golden Temple in Amritsar for Sikhs, dargahs such as Ajmer Sharif, and churches such as Velankanni.
Pilgrimage (tirtha yatra) brought people from distant regions together for centuries, spreading languages, stories, food, crafts and trade and creating a sense that the whole land is connected.
One place can be sacred to several traditions — Mount Kailash is revered by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of the Bon tradition.

Sacred groves (devrai, kavu, sarna, orans) and sacred rivers show how reverence can protect nature; today pollution and crowding are challenges, and caring for these places means keeping them clean and respecting everyone's beliefs.

skills.title: Explain why a society needs a government and rules
Describe the main forms of government: monarchy (absolute and constitutional), democracy (direct and representative), dictatorship, theocracy, oligarchy

expectations: A government is needed to make rules and decisions for everyone, keep order and safety, settle disputes and provide services such as schools, roads and health care.

In a monarchy a king or queen rules by birth; in an absolute monarchy the ruler has almost all power, while in a constitutional monarchy the monarch is head of state but elected representatives make the laws.

In a democracy power comes from the people: in a direct democracy citizens vote on decisions themselves (as in ancient Athens); in a representative democracy, like India, citizens elect representatives.

In a dictatorship one person or a small group takes and keeps power, often by force, and does not allow criticism; in a theocracy religious leaders rule according to religious law; in an oligarchy a small group holds power.

Democracy is more than voting: it also needs equal rights for all, the rule of law, freedom of speech and a free press, courts that can check the government, protection of minorities, and leaders who can be questioned and voted out.

expectations: A constitution is the basic rulebook of a country: it sets up the government, divides and limits its powers, and lists the rights and duties of citizens; all other laws must follow it.

India's Constitution was written by the Constituent Assembly, which first met on 9 December 1946; Dr Rajendra Prasad was its President and Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; members came from many regions and communities, including 15 women.
It was adopted on 26 November 1949 (celebrated as Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 January 1950 (celebrated as Republic Day), after almost three years of debate.

The Preamble begins "We, the people of India" — power comes from the people; it calls India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic, and aims to secure justice, liberty, equality and fraternity for all (the words socialist and secular were added in 1976).

The Constitution gives Fundamental Rights (like equality, freedom and education) and Fundamental Duties, divides work among the legislature (makes laws), the executive (carries them out) and the judiciary (interprets laws and protects rights), and can be amended through a careful process.

expectations: Barter is swapping goods or services directly without money; it works only when each person wants what the other has (a double coincidence of wants), and it lacks a common measure of value, cannot easily divide big items like a cow, and many goods spoil.

Over time people used commodity money (grain, cattle, salt, cowrie shells), then metal coins (in India the punch-marked coins of around the 6th century BCE), then paper notes, bank money (cheques, cards) and now digital payments such as UPI (launched in 2016).
Money is a medium of exchange (accepted by everyone for buying and selling), a measure of value (prices in rupees let us compare things) and a store of value (it can be saved and used later).

A rupee note has value not because of its paper but because people trust it and the law makes it legal tender; in India the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes and the Government of India issues coins.
With digital money, payment moves from one bank account to another; it is safe only if you never share your PIN or OTP and check whom you are paying.

skills.title: Identify different kinds of markets (weekly haat, neighbourhood shops, wholesale mandi, malls, online) and their features
Trace the chain from producer to consumer and the role of wholesalers, retailers and middlemen
Explain how demand and supply affect prices
Act as an informed consumer: MRP, bills, quality marks and consumer rights

expectations: A market is any arrangement where buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods or services for money — a weekly haat, a neighbourhood shop, a wholesale mandi, a shopping mall, or an online marketplace with no physical place at all.

Goods usually pass along a chain: producer (farmer or factory) → wholesaler (buys in bulk, e.g. at a mandi) → retailer (shop, sabziwala) → consumer; each step adds costs such as transport, storage, rent and profit.

Prices depend on demand and supply: when supply falls (e.g. heavy rain destroys tomatoes) or demand rises (e.g. festival shopping), prices tend to rise; when supply is plentiful or demand falls, prices tend to fall.

Different markets suit different needs: haats are cheaper because sellers have low costs and often sell their own produce; malls offer variety and comfort but with higher costs; online markets offer convenience and home delivery.

An informed consumer checks the MRP (the maximum retail price — a shop cannot charge more), asks for a bill, looks for quality marks (ISI, AGMARK, FSSAI, BIS hallmark for gold) and knows they can complain under consumer protection law.

misconceptions.belief: Prices are set by the shopkeeper alone and do not depend on how much is available or wanted.
signs: Says tomatoes got costly because "the shopkeeper is greedy"
Cannot predict how a festival or a flood changes prices

workedExample.problem: Tomato prices in a city jumped from ₹30/kg to ₹80/kg in two weeks after floods. Explain why, step by step.
steps: Supply: floods damaged fields and blocked roads, so far fewer tomatoes reached the mandi
Demand: families still needed tomatoes for daily cooking, so demand stayed about the same
Competition: many buyers chased fewer tomatoes, so sellers could ask higher prices
Chain costs: longer, harder transport and more spoiled tomatoes added to costs at each step
Conclusion: lower supply + steady demand + higher costs → a sharp price rise; prices should fall again as new harvests arrive

skills.title: Trace the history of farming in India on a timeline (early farming at Mehrgarh, Harappan farming, ancient irrigation, the Green Revolution)
Classify crops by season (kharif, rabi, zaid) and link the seasons to the monsoon
Explain traditional and modern ways of farming and irrigating
Explain challenges farmers face today and possible solutions

expectations: Farming in the subcontinent is very old: at Mehrgarh (in present-day Pakistan) people grew wheat and barley and kept animals around 7000 BCE; Harappan farmers grew wheat, barley and cotton and used ploughs.
Ancient Indians built clever irrigation: wells, tanks, stepwells and canals; the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri, linked to the Chola king Karikala around the 2nd century CE, is still in use.

Indian crops follow seasons: kharif crops (rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra, groundnut) are sown with the monsoon around June–July and harvested around September–October; rabi crops (wheat, mustard, gram, barley, peas) are sown around October–December and harvested around March–April; zaid crops (watermelon, cucumber) grow in the short summer season.

The Green Revolution of the 1960s used high-yielding seeds, irrigation and fertilisers to make India self-sufficient in food grains, especially wheat and rice in Punjab and Haryana, but it also led to overuse of groundwater and chemicals in some places.

Farmers today face small landholdings, dependence on an uncertain monsoon, falling groundwater, damaged soil, price swings and climate change; solutions include water-saving methods like drip irrigation, crop diversity including millets, soil testing, organic and natural farming, and insurance and fair prices.

skills.title: Locate India's neighbouring countries on a map and state their direction from India
Describe shared physical geography: the Himalayas, seas, and rivers that cross borders
Describe shared history and culture between India and its neighbours
Explain why cooperation with neighbours matters (rivers, trade, disasters, regional groups)

expectations: India shares land borders with Pakistan and Afghanistan (north-west), China (north and north-east), Nepal and Bhutan (north), and Bangladesh and Myanmar (east); its sea neighbours are Sri Lanka (south, across the narrow Palk Strait) and the Maldives (south-west).
The Himalayas run along India's northern border with Nepal, Bhutan and China; India's longest land border is with Bangladesh.

Big rivers cross borders: the Indus begins in Tibet, flows through Ladakh and on through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea; the Brahmaputra begins in Tibet (Yarlung Tsangpo), enters Arunachal Pradesh, flows through Assam and into Bangladesh; the Ganga flows into Bangladesh as the Padma.

India and its neighbours share history and culture: Buddhism links Lumbini (Nepal), Bodh Gaya (India) and Sri Lanka, Bhutan and Myanmar; languages like Bengali, Punjabi, Nepali and Tamil are spoken on both sides of borders; Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.
Neighbours need cooperation on shared rivers and floods, trade, transport, tourism and disasters; regional groups such as SAARC (formed in 1985 with eight members) were created to encourage this.

skills.title: Place the major kingdoms of the 6th–10th centuries on a map and timeline, and name centuries correctly (e.g. 606 CE is in the 7th century)
Explain the rivalries and conflicts of the period (Harsha and Pulakeshin II, Pallavas and Chalukyas, the struggle for Kanauj)
Describe the contributions of these kingdoms to temples, learning and literature
Use inscriptions and travellers' accounts as evidence, and check one against another

expectations: Between the 6th and 10th centuries many powerful kingdoms existed at the same time: Harsha ruled from Kanauj in the north (606–647 CE); the Chalukyas from Badami (Vatapi) in the Deccan; the Pallavas from Kanchipuram in the south; later the Rashtrakutas in the Deccan, the Palas in Bengal and Bihar and the Gurjara-Pratiharas in the north and west.

Rivalries shaped the period: the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha near the Narmada (recorded in the Aihole inscription); Pallavas and Chalukyas fought repeatedly; the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas fought for control of rich Kanauj (the "tripartite struggle").

These kingdoms built remarkable temples: Pallava rock-cut rathas and the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram; Chalukya temples at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal; the Rashtrakuta Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock from the top down.

Learning and literature flourished: Nalanda drew students from across Asia, and the Palas founded Vikramashila; Banabhatta wrote the Harshacharita about Harsha; Tamil devotional poets (Alvars and Nayanars) composed hymns; Kannada literature grew under the Rashtrakutas.

Our sources include inscriptions written by court poets (like the Aihole inscription) and travellers' accounts (like the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang's); each has a point of view, so historians compare them.

skills.title: Describe the Chola empire under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I (temples, conquests, navy)
Explain Chola village self-government and Chola bronze art
Describe the raids and invasions from the north-west and the other regional kingdoms of the period, in order on a timeline

expectations: In the south the Cholas grew into a great power: Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur (completed around 1010 CE), and Rajendra I led armies to the Ganga, founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram and sent a navy to Southeast Asia (around 1025 CE) to protect trade.

Chola villages had assemblies (sabha, ur); inscriptions at Uttaramerur describe choosing members by lot (kudavolai) from qualified candidates; Chola artists made famous bronze images such as Nataraja by the lost-wax method.

In the north-west, Mahmud of Ghazni raided north India many times between about 1000 and 1027 CE, carrying off wealth (including from the Somnath temple in 1025–26) without ruling most of India; later Muhammad Ghori lost the First Battle of Tarain (1191) to Prithviraj Chauhan but won the second (1192), which led to the Delhi Sultanate being founded in 1206.

Other regional kingdoms flourished: the Chandelas built the Khajuraho temples, the Paramara king Bhoja was a scholar-king in Malwa, the Solankis built the Modhera Sun temple in Gujarat, and the Hoysalas built temples at Belur and Halebidu.

The scholar Al-Biruni came with Mahmud, learned Sanskrit and wrote a detailed book on India (Kitab-ul-Hind); historians compare such accounts with inscriptions and other sources, since each has its own point of view; "turning tides" means power was shifting in several regions at once.

skills.title: Describe communities who came to India and settled, and where and roughly when they arrived
Explain why they came (trade, safety, faith) and how they were received
Explain how these communities and India's own many traditions enriched shared culture
Interpret stories and sources about their arrival and explain why living together in diversity matters

expectations: Over many centuries people from other lands settled in India and made it home: Jewish communities on the Kerala coast (Kochi) and the Konkan, Christians in Kerala (tradition links them to St Thomas in the 1st century CE), Arab traders and early Muslim communities on the Malabar coast, Parsis (Zoroastrians from Persia) in Gujarat, Siddis of African origin, Armenians, and in 1959 Tibetans.
Many came by sea to the busy west-coast ports for trade, helped by the monsoon winds; others, like the Parsis and the Tibetans, came seeking safety to practise their faith.
Local rulers often welcomed them: Kerala rulers gave copper-plate grants with rights and privileges to Jewish and Christian communities, and a Gujarat ruler allowed the Parsis to settle at Sanjan.

These communities kept their faiths while adopting local languages, dress and food (Parsis speak Gujarati; Kerala's Jews and Christians speak Malayalam), and enriched India's culture, business, science and food — alongside traditions that began in India itself, such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism.

Stories such as the Parsi "milk and sugar" tale, recorded centuries later, express the idea of newcomers blending in and sweetening society; India's strength has long been many communities living and working together.

skills.title: Distinguish the state (territory, people, government, sovereignty) from the government that runs it
Describe the three organs and the three levels of government in India
Explain how government touches daily life from birth to adulthood and how it is paid for
Explain how citizens take part in and hold the government accountable

expectations: A state (country) has four features: a population, a territory with borders, a government and sovereignty (it makes its own decisions); the state is lasting, while the government — the people and bodies running it — changes, for example after elections.

The government has three organs: the legislature makes laws (Parliament, state assemblies), the executive carries them out (ministers, civil servants, police) and the judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes (courts).

India has three levels of government: the Union (whole country — defence, railways, currency), the states (police, state roads, many hospitals and schools) and local bodies (panchayats in villages, municipalities in towns — water, streetlights, cleanliness), with local bodies strengthened by constitutional amendments in 1992.

Government touches life from birth: birth certificates, vaccinations, schooling (free education for ages 6–14), ration cards, roads, Aadhaar, the right to vote at 18 and driving licences; these services are paid for mainly by taxes that people and businesses pay, including taxes on things we buy.

Citizens shape the government by voting, attending gram sabhas or ward meetings, using the Right to Information, filing complaints, and speaking up peacefully, and they also have duties towards the country and each other.

skills.title: Define infrastructure and classify it as physical (roads, railways, ports, power, water, telecom and digital) or social (schools, hospitals)
Explain, as a cause-and-effect chain, how infrastructure drives development
Describe key milestones in India's infrastructure
Weigh the costs and trade-offs of infrastructure and the need for maintenance and sustainability

expectations: Infrastructure is the basic set of facilities and systems that a country needs to function: physical infrastructure (roads, railways, ports, airports, electricity, water supply, telecom and digital networks) and social infrastructure (schools, hospitals, sanitation).

Infrastructure is an engine of development: a road, power line or internet connection lets farmers reach markets, children reach schools, patients reach hospitals, factories get supplies and new jobs and businesses appear.

India's milestones include the first passenger train from Bori Bunder (Mumbai) to Thane on 16 April 1853, the Konkan Railway through the Western Ghats, the Golden Quadrilateral highways linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, metro rail in many cities, the Chenab rail bridge in Jammu and Kashmir, and digital networks such as UPI.

Infrastructure has costs and trade-offs: land must be acquired, people may be displaced, forests and rivers can be harmed; good planning includes fair compensation, resettlement, environmental checks and listening to affected communities.
Infrastructure needs regular maintenance and should be sustainable — for example solar power, metro rail that reduces traffic pollution, and rainwater harvesting.

skills.title: Explain what banks do (keep deposits safe, give loans, pay and charge interest, make payments) and the role of the Reserve Bank of India
Compare savings accounts, fixed deposits, recurring deposits and loans

expectations: A bank accepts deposits and keeps them safe, lends money to people and businesses, and helps with payments; it pays interest to depositors and charges higher interest to borrowers, and the difference covers its costs and profit.

The money people deposit is not kept as the same notes in a locker: banks keep part as a reserve and lend the rest, so one person's savings help another person build a house or start a business — the "magic" of finance.

A savings account lets you withdraw any time and earns some interest; a fixed deposit locks money for a fixed period at a higher interest rate; a recurring deposit saves a fixed amount every month; a loan must be repaid with interest.
Simple interest = Principal × Rate × Time ÷ 100; for example, ₹1,000 at 5% per year for 2 years earns ₹100, giving ₹1,100 in all.

The Reserve Bank of India (set up in 1935) is the central bank that issues notes and regulates banks; schemes like the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) opened zero-balance accounts so that everyone can bank; safe banking means never sharing your PIN, OTP or password.
